title: Working with Buyers: Consultations, Showings & Agency in Practice
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

options: After the buyer has seen several properties
Before showing any property
Only when the buyer is ready to write an offer
At the closing table
rationales: Showing first means agency, financing, and criteria are all unresolved while the agent is already working.
Correct. The consultation establishes agency in writing, verifies financing, lets the buyer define criteria, and sets expectations — all of which must precede showings.
Waiting until offer time wastes months and leaves the relationship undefined.
The consultation is the first meeting, not the last.

questions.stem: A lender letter based on income and assets the borrower stated but the lender never verified is a:
options: Preapproval
Prequalification
Loan commitment
Clear to close
rationales: Preapproval requires the lender to verify income, assets, and credit.
Correct. A prequalification rests on unverified stated information and is weak evidence of ability to close, whatever the letter's title says.
A loan commitment is final underwriting approval near the end of escrow.
Clear to close is the final step before funding.

questions.stem: A buyer's agent should advise removing the loan contingency when:
options: The lender says the file 'looks good'
Underwriting has approved the file in writing
The appraisal has been ordered
The contingency deadline arrives
rationales: Informal reassurance is not approval, and files die after it constantly.
Correct. Removal should follow written underwriting approval — if financing fails after removal, the buyer is in default and faces liquidated damages up to 3% of the price.
Ordering an appraisal says nothing about the borrower's underwriting status.
A deadline arriving is a reason to seek an extension or deliver a removal, not a reason to remove without approval.

questions.stem: During a showing an agent notices ceiling staining with fresh paint around it. The buyer says it does not matter. The agent must:
options: Accept the buyer's decision and say nothing
Disclose the observation in writing and recommend a qualified inspection
Diagnose the likely cause for the buyer
Report the seller to the DRE
rationales: The visual inspection duty is the agent's own and is not waived by the buyer's enthusiasm.
Correct. Observe, disclose, refer — put the observation in writing the same day and recommend inspection of that area, then document if the buyer declines.
Agents are not inspectors and must not diagnose cause or estimate cost.
The immediate duty is disclosure to the buyer, not a regulatory complaint.

questions.stem: At an open house, the listing agent asks a buyer's agent about her clients' timeline and approval amount. Sharing that information would:
options: Build useful rapport between agents
Breach the duty of confidentiality owed to the buyer
Be required by the duty of honesty to third parties
Be permissible if the buyer never finds out
rationales: Rapport is useful, but not at the cost of the client's negotiating position.
Correct. Urgency and a maximum approval amount are confidential client information; disclosing them hands the seller leverage and is actionable if it costs the buyer money.
Honesty to third parties does not require volunteering the client's confidential information.
The breach occurs regardless of whether the client learns of it.

questions.stem: A listing is tenant-occupied with a 24-hour notice requirement. The seller tells the agent to show it immediately. The agent should:
options: Show it, because the owner consented
Wait for proper notice, because the seller cannot waive the tenant's entry rights
Show it if the tenant appears to be away
Show it and leave a note
rationales: Ownership does not override the tenant's right of possession.
Correct. Entry generally requires reasonable written notice with 24 hours presumed reasonable; the seller cannot waive the tenant's rights, and the buyer is about to inherit this relationship.
Absence does not create a right of entry.
A note after the fact does not satisfy an advance notice requirement.

questions.stem: A buyer asks whether they can add a second unit to a property. The agent should:
options: Give an opinion based on the lot size
Refer the buyer to the city planning department
State that state law now permits it everywhere
Confirm it is allowed if neighbors have done it
rationales: Lot size is one of many factors and an agent opinion here invites reliance the agent cannot support.
Correct. Zoning, permitting, and feasibility questions belong to the planning department; the agent's role is to route the buyer to the authority that can actually answer.
State housing law has expanded unit allowances but application varies by parcel and jurisdiction; a blanket claim is a misrepresentation.
A neighbor's structure may be nonconforming, unpermitted, or approved under different rules.

questions.stem: A lender offers a buyer's agent a $400 payment for each client referred who closes a loan. Accepting it would:
options: Be lawful if disclosed to the buyer
Violate RESPA's prohibition on compensation for referrals of settlement services
Be lawful because the agent is not a lender
Be lawful if the buyer chose the lender independently
rationales: Disclosure does not cure a prohibited referral fee.
Correct. RESPA prohibits giving or accepting anything of value for referring settlement service business; only payment for services actually performed at fair market value is permitted.
The prohibition applies to anyone giving or receiving the payment, not only to lenders.
The payment is compensation for the referral regardless of how the buyer made the choice.

questions.stem: During the consultation, the agent should establish the buyer's search criteria by:
options: Recommending neighborhoods that suit the buyer's background
Asking the buyer to define their own criteria
Selecting areas the agent knows best
Narrowing to areas where similar buyers have purchased
rationales: Inferring where a buyer belongs from their background is steering.
Correct. Letting clients define their own criteria is simultaneously better service and the agent's fair housing protection.
Agent convenience is not a legitimate basis for limiting a buyer's options.
Steering buyers toward areas where 'similar' buyers bought uses protected characteristics as a proxy.

questions.stem: A buyer asks whether a neighborhood is safe. The agent should:
options: Give an honest personal assessment
Provide published crime data sources for the buyer to evaluate
Say the area is safe if the agent believes it is
Refuse to discuss the neighborhood in any way
rationales: A personal assessment about safety is both an unverifiable factual claim and a steering risk.
Correct. Direct the buyer to objective published sources so they evaluate the area themselves — compliant and more genuinely useful.
Characterizing an area as safe is a representation the agent cannot support.
A bare refusal disserves the client; the redirect to data is what makes the response work.

questions.stem: A buyer instructs the agent to waive the inspection contingency against the agent's advice. The agent should:
options: Refuse to write the offer
Write it as instructed and document the advice given in writing the same day
Write it and say nothing further
Write it but secretly retain the contingency
rationales: Waiving inspections is lawful; the buyer is entitled to make that choice.
Correct. Obedience covers lawful instructions, and a same-day email confirming what was advised and that the buyer elected otherwise is the agent's file if a defect surfaces later.
Failing to document contrary advice leaves the agent exposed when the buyer later says they were never warned.
Altering the buyer's instructions without authorization breaches the duty of obedience.

questions.stem: The strongest evidence a buyer can attach to an offer regarding financing is a letter showing the lender has:
options: Spoken with the buyer by phone
Verified income, assets, and credit
Estimated a payment amount
Received the purchase contract
rationales: A conversation produces a prequalification at best.
Correct. Verification of income, assets, and credit is what distinguishes a preapproval from a prequalification and what a seller is actually evaluating.
A payment estimate reflects no underwriting review.
Receiving the contract happens after the offer and says nothing about the borrower.

questions.stem: Agents should assume that occupied listings may have:
options: No recording devices, since that would be illegal
Audio and video recording devices in use
Recording only in common areas
Recording only with posted notice
rationales: Video recording of one's own property is common and often lawful; audio raises separate legal questions but devices are frequently present.
Correct. Assume every occupied property may be recording, and never discuss a buyer's budget, enthusiasm, or strategy inside it.
Devices are commonly placed throughout a home, not only in common areas.
Notice is not always posted, and the practical rule is to assume recording regardless.

questions.stem: A buyer asks the agent to omit from the offer that the buyer is an investor who intends to rent the property. The agent should:
options: Comply, because investor status is not protected
Decline, because concealing a material fact from the other party is fraudulent
Comply if the seller does not ask
Comply and note it in the file
rationales: Investor status is not a protected characteristic, but that is not the issue — active concealment is.
Correct. Misrepresenting or concealing the buyer's identity or intent from the seller is fraud, not a negotiating tactic, and the agent owes third parties honesty.
The absence of a question does not license concealment of a material fact.
Documenting participation in concealment does not cure it.

questions.stem: A buyer asks how they should hold title. The agent should:
options: Recommend joint tenancy for its probate avoidance
Explain that options exist and refer the buyer to an attorney or CPA
Instruct escrow to select the most common local vesting
Recommend a trust for asset protection
rationales: Recommending a specific vesting is giving legal advice beyond a licensee's authority.
Correct. A licensee may describe the options generally but must refer the choice to an attorney or CPA, because vesting carries legal, estate, and tax consequences.
Delegating a client's legal decision to escrow based on local habit does not cure the advice problem.
Recommending a trust is legal advice and may also implicate tax planning.

questions.stem: In a slow market, a hesitant buyer asks whether prices will fall further. The agent should:
options: Predict the direction of the market confidently
Present inventory, days on market, and sale-to-list data and let the buyer decide
Urge the buyer to act before prices rise
Decline to provide any market information
rationales: Market predictions cannot be supported and clients remember them.
Correct. Present what the data shows and let the buyer decide; pressuring a hesitant buyer into a purchase they regret costs a career of referrals for one commission.
Urgency claims the agent cannot substantiate are misrepresentations.
Withholding market data disserves the client — the issue is forecasting, not informing.

questions.stem: Under a buyer representation agreement, if the seller's side contributes less compensation than the buyer agreed to pay the buyer's broker, typically:
options: The broker absorbs the shortfall
The buyer owes the difference under the agreement
The seller must increase the contribution
The transaction cannot close
rationales: The written agreement between buyer and broker governs the broker's compensation.
Correct. Buyer representation agreements generally make the buyer responsible for any shortfall, which is why the agent must explain the compensation structure clearly at consultation.
The seller has no obligation beyond what the seller agreed to contribute.
A compensation shortfall is a payment question, not an obstacle to closing.

questions.stem: The professional posture summarized as 'observe, disclose, refer' means the agent should:
options: Diagnose the problem, estimate the cost, and recommend a contractor
State what was observed, put it in writing, and recommend a qualified expert
Note concerns verbally and wait for the buyer's inspector to find them
Avoid commenting on condition to limit liability
rationales: Diagnosis and cost estimation exceed a licensee's expertise and create liability.
Correct. The agent reports the observation in writing and routes the client to someone qualified to evaluate it — the standard that satisfies the visual inspection duty without overstepping.
Relying on the inspector to find it does not satisfy the agent's independent disclosure duty.
Silence about an observed material fact is the violation, not a liability strategy.
